The Common shiner (Luxilus cornutus) is a cyprinid species native to the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence River basins, where it occupies clear, gravel-bottomed streams and small rivers. Field surveys have documented that this species attains a maximum recorded total length of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters], a size that distinguishes it from many smaller congeneric species within the Luxilus clade. Egg diameter measurements from gravid females collected in spring spawning runs indicate a diameter of approximately 1.25 mm, from which the wet weight at birth is estimated at 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], reflecting the modest initial investment in yolk reserves typical of lithophilic spawning minnows. The eggs are demersal and adhesive, adhering to the interstices of stream gravel where they undergo a period of incubation. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larvae remain within the gravel matrix for several days before emerging as free-swimming exogenously feeding larvae, a critical transition that depends on adequate dissolved oxygen and stable thermal regimes in the natal riffle.

Juvenile Common shiner grow rapidly during their first summer, and comparative growth studies indicate that puberty is attained at a total length of 7.4 centimeters [Lp = 7.4 centimeters], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 4.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 4.4 grams]. This length at maturation is consistent with values reported for other gravel-spawning cyprinids from similar latitudes. The age at which this developmental milestone is reached has been studied under controlled laboratory conditions; when reared at a constant water temperature of 21.9 °C [T = 21.9 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 730 days [tp = 730 days]. This relatively long juvenile period likely reflects the energetic demands of the cool-water environment and the need to accumulate sufficient lipid reserves before the onset of gonadal recrudescence. The onset of sexual maturation is accompanied by the development of tubercles on the head and opercles of males, a secondary sexual characteristic observed during the prespawning period.

Once individuals have reached reproductive maturity, adult body condition continues to improve, and the species exhibits a maximum recorded adult body mass of 71 grams [Wwi = 71 grams] in the wild, a value derived from large-bodied individuals collected from productive stream reaches. This ultimate wet weight of 71 grams [Wwi = 71 grams] is achieved only after several years of growth and is considerably greater than the mass at puberty, illustrating the substantial somatic investment that occurs between maturation and asymptotic body size. Comparative data from museum specimen series demonstrate that the length-weight relationship in this species is strongly allometric, with larger individuals exhibiting disproportionately greater mass, a pattern common among cyprinids that occupy stable lotic environments. The ultimate total length of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters] serves as the asymptotic value for this population, beyond which further linear growth is negligible, although weight gain may continue marginally in the largest age classes.

Longevity in the Common shiner has been assessed through otolith-based age estimation in populations inhabiting southern Ontario streams. When maintained under natural thermal regimes that approximate a mean annual temperature of 21.9 °C [T = 21.9 °C], the maximum recorded life span is 3285 days [am = 3285 days], or approximately nine years, making this species relatively long-lived among North American cyprinids of comparable body size. This extended life span is unusual for a fish of this maximum total length of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters] and likely reflects the low natural mortality rates characteristic of stable, predator-limited headwater stream habitats. Survivorship curves derived from mark-recapture studies indicate that adult mortality remains low until approximately six years of age, after which a gradual senescence-related decline becomes apparent. The oldest individuals are typically those occupying the most productive stream reaches, suggesting that habitat quality exerts a strong influence on realized longevity in this species.

Reproductive ecology in the Common shiner is characterized by multiple spawning events during the spring and early summer, with females depositing adhesive eggs over clean gravel in shallow riffles. A single reproductively active female can produce between 200 and 400 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 200 and 400 eggs per spawning event], and field observations indicate that most individuals participate in two to three spawning events each breeding season [F_R_i = two to three spawning events each breeding season]. This iteroparous strategy, combined with the relatively small egg size corresponding to a wet weight at birth of 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], allows the species to spread reproductive risk across multiple clutches and variable stream discharge conditions. The reproductively viable adult population, which includes individuals from the time of puberty onward, experiences natural mortality primarily through predation by piscivorous birds and larger centrarchids. Spawning adults exhibit nest-guarding behavior, with males defending small territories over cleaned gravel patches, a social structure that contributes to the species' reproductive success in crowded stream habitats.
